---
title: "Why the other queue always moves faster"
description: "It does not. You only notice the times it does, because losing to the other lane hurts more than winning feels good."
author: "Mesfin Genie"
date: "2026-09-16"
categories: [behavioural economics, everyday]
---

You pick a lane at the supermarket. The lane next to you starts moving. You
switch. Your old lane moves. Everyone has lived this, and everyone believes
the universe is doing it to them personally.

The universe is not. Over a year, your lane and the other lane move at about
the same rate. What differs is what you remember.

When your lane wins, nothing happens. You reach the till, pay, leave. There is
nothing to notice, so you notice nothing. When the other lane wins, you stand
there watching someone who arrived after you walk out before you. That is a
small loss with a face on it, and losses with faces stick.

So the memory is skewed by design. You have a full record of every time you
lost and almost no record of the times you won. Ask yourself the last time
your lane clearly beat the other one. You will struggle, and it happened about
half the time.

This matters beyond queues. It is why people are sure they always get the slow
train, the bad seat, the referee who hates their team. The losses are counted
and the wins are not. It is worth knowing about yourself because the feeling
of being unlucky is often a feeling of being human with a normal memory.

The queue is fine. Stay in it.
